text: Catherine Sue Opie, born in 1961 in Sandusky, Ohio, is an American fine art photographer and educator who lives and works in Los Angeles. She earned a Bachelor of Arts from the San Francisco Art Institute in 1985 and a Master of Fine Arts from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) in 1988, where she was a strictly black-and-white photographer before transitioning to color work. Opie's early artistic development began when she received a Kodak Instamatic camera on her 9th birthday and created her first photograph—a self-portrait making muscles—followed by establishing her own darkroom at age 14. Her family moved to California in 1975, and in 1988, she moved to Los Angeles, where she worked as a lab technician at the University of California, Irvine, while also setting up working studios with her former partner, painter Julie Burleigh, in South Central Los Angeles. Her work explores the connections between mainstream and marginalized societies, focusing on portraiture, studio, and landscape photography to examine sexual identity, community, and the American dream. She is known for her portraits of the Los Angeles leather-dyke community, including the series *Being and Having* (1991) and *Portraits* (1993–1997), which depict queer identities such as drag kings, cross-dressers, and F-to-M transexuals, drawing visual references to 17th-century Old Master portraiture and using symbolic elements like blood in works such as *Self Portrait/Pervert* (1994) and *Self-portrait/Cutting* (1993). Opie's work also includes the *American Cities* (1997–present) series of panoramic black-and-white photographs of American cities and the *Domestic* (1995–1998) series documenting lesbian families on an RV road trip. She has curated exhibitions, including a selection of Tony Greene’s work at the 2014 Whitney Biennial with Richard Hawkins, and has served on the Artist Council and board of overseers at the Hammer Museum, as well as on the board of the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, and the Andy Warhol Foundation. In 2011, she photographed Elizabeth Taylor’s home in Bel Air, Los Angeles, taking 3,000 images with 129 forming the completed study, published as *700 Nimes Road*. Her first film, *The Modernist* (2017), composed of 800 still images, features Pig Pen (Stosh Fila) as a protagonist and is described as both an ode to Los Angeles and a critique of American modernism. Opie has used a range of printing technologies, including Chronochrome, Iris prints, Polaroids, and silver photogravure, and has referenced art history through bright color backgrounds (alluding to Hans Holbein) and frontal full-body portraits (inspired by August Sander), as seen in *Self Portrait/Nursing* (2004). She teaches photography at the University of California, Los Angeles, where she was named the inaugural endowed chair in 2019, funded by a $2-million gift from Lynda and Stewart Resnick. Opie has also taught at Anderson Ranch Arts Center and the Fine Arts Work Center. Her work balances personal and political themes, emphasizing community, identity, and the role of architecture, and she has explored controversial topics influenced by photographers like Robert Mapplethorpe and Nan Goldin. Her name appears in the lyrics of the Le Tigre song "Hot Topic." Her work is held in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, and she has received awards including the United States Artists Fellowship (2006) and the President’s Award for Lifetime Achievement from the Women’s Caucus for Art (2009).
